data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological evolution has no conscious aim, whereas Popperian science has the explicit regulative ideal of truth.","Natural selection is blind, while the scientist's preference is a deliberate rational commitment.","Evolutionary fitness is relative to a specific environment, while corroboration aims at universal laws."],"overturn_conditions":["If the goal of science is redefined away from truth (e.g., to mere instrumental prediction), the analogy and the defense collapse.","If past performance is shown to be logically irrelevant to even a conjectural estimate of future performance in a way that breaks the 'severe test' logic."],"shared_structure":["Selection operates on past performance without guaranteeing future survival.","The 'fittest' or 'best-corroborated' entity is chosen procedurally, not because it is proven to be the ultimate truth/survivor.","The process is rational relative to a goal (survival/truth) despite lacking inductive certainty."],"source_memory_refs":["evolutionary_selection_process"],"transfer_claims":["Just as organisms are selected based on past survival without a guarantee of future fitness, theories are preferred based on past corroboration without a guarantee of future truth.","The rationality of the choice lies in the alignment with the system's goal (survival/truth), not in a predictive proof."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is more likely true, but as a rational procedural rule grounded in the metaphysical aim of science (verisimilitude) and the logical asymmetry of falsification; however, accepting this defense costs the scientist any guarantee that the preferred theory is actually closer to the truth, reducing the preference to a 'rational gamble' rather than an epistemic certainty.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the concept of verisimilitude is formally incoherent (as argued by Miller and Tich\u00fd), then the metaphysical aim grounding the preference collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference cannot be distinguished from a pragmatic necessity without a normative reason, then it fails to be a rational defense and becomes mere habit.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If surviving severe tests provides no logical basis for expecting future success even as a conjecture, then the preference is arbitrary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument reconstructs Popper's distinction between 'probability' (inductive support) and 'corroboration' (logical report of past test performance). It posits that preferring the better-corroborated theory is rational because, given the goal of finding true theories (verisimilitude), the theory that has survived the severest tests is the one that has done the most to expose itself to falsification and failed. This is not an inductive leap that it will survive future tests, but a strategic choice based on the only available evidence of its empirical content. The mechanism addresses the 'smuggling induction' charge by reframing the preference as a methodological imperative derived from the definition of scientific progress, not a probabilistic calculation.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
